title: Congenital malformations
objectives: Classify ARM, cloaca and Hirschsprung variants with the operation each demands.
State Todani classification and the operation for choledochal cyst.
Outline biliary atresia workup and Kasai timing with outcome predictors.
body_md:
### Why this area matters

Malformations are the surgeon's home ground and the exam's backbone: ARM/cloaca, Hirschsprung, biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, malrotation, duplications, Meckel diverticulum. Classification systems are free marks — write every one you know, correctly.

### Hindgut and midgut

ARM: high versus low by the puborectalis sling, with pouch colon as the Indian-exam favourite — single-stage versus staged pull-through, and continence as the lifelong metric. Persistent cloaca: common channel length decides complexity; hydrocolpos needs drainage now, reconstruction later, with multidisciplinary follow-up. Hirschsprung: transition zone, biopsy, pull-through choices, and the postoperative triad of obstruction, enterocolitis and soiling. Malrotation: bilious vomiting is volvulus until proven otherwise — upper GI contrast, then Ladd procedure without delay.

### Hepatobiliary

Biliary atresia: persistent pale stools and conjugated jaundice beyond two weeks, HIDA non-excretion, liver biopsy and intraoperative cholangiogram; Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days changes the curve, with clearance of jaundice as the early predictor. Choledochal cyst: Todani I–V (type I and IVa dominate questions), complete excision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy — never internal drainage alone — because of the malignancy risk. Bilirubin metabolism (conjugation, enterohepatic circulation) underpins both answers.

### Duplications, Meckel, atresias

Alimentary duplications share wall and blood supply with native bowel — excise without devascularising the host. Meckel: rule of twos, painless bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa, technetium scan. Jejunoileal atresias: the Grosfeld-type spectrum and tapering enteroplasty versus resection choices.

### How it is asked

Classification → embryology one-liner → workup → operation → complications → follow-up. Draw the classification table first; it anchors the rest.
